lessons.title: 9. 气体、液体和固体的结构

nearbyText:
Yakov I. Frenkel ($1894\sim1952$) was a Soviet theoretical physicist who worked in several areas of physics.
The source credits him with creating modern liquid theory, laying foundations of ferromagnetic theory, and developing the first quantitative theory of uranium nuclear fission.

The source also describes his work on atmospheric electricity and the origin of Earth's magnetic field.
These statements preserve the textbook's historical attribution;
labels such as "creator" and "first" are not presented as independently verified, exclusive historical conclusions.

Liquid molecules are close together.
The source explains compression in terms of molecular deformation (Figure $9$);

a more careful explanation is that short-range repulsion increases sharply as molecular spacing is reduced further.
Further compression usually requires a large force, so liquids have low, but not zero, compressibility.
This resistance should not be understood only as literal deformation of the molecules themselves.

A liquid can flow and has no fixed shape.
In the approximate cage-and-hopping picture, an isotropic liquid at rest with no directional driving has equal opportunities for rearrangements in all directions, with no overall directed flow (Figure $8$).

With an unbalanced driving influence, such as gravity or pressure from a moving solid, this picture describes flow as a slight bias of rearrangements in the driving direction (Figure $10$).
Continuing rearrangements allow the liquid to flow and, under usual conditions, take the shape of its container.
